topic: Braced Initialization's Preference for Initializer-List Constructors
explanation:
Braced initialization is not merely a syntactic alternative to parentheses; it has distinct semantic implications during constructor overload resolution. Specifically, if a class has one or more constructors that accept a `std::initializer_list`, the compiler will strongly prefer them when the object is created using braced initializers.

Scott Meyers presents this as a critical drawback and a source of surprising behavior. The key insight is that this preference for `std::initializer_list` constructors can override what might otherwise be a better-matching constructor based on argument types. This means that introducing an `initializer_list` constructor to a class can silently change the behavior of existing client code that uses braced initialization.

The mechanics behind this involve a special two-stage process for overload resolution. When encountering a braced-init-list, the compiler first searches exclusively for constructors taking a `std::initializer_list`. If it finds any, it will attempt to match the arguments to one of them, even if this requires type conversions. Only if no `std::initializer_list` constructor can be made to work will the compiler proceed to the second stage and consider all other constructors in a normal overload resolution process.

This has significant practical implications, most famously with standard containers. For example, creating a `std::vector` with two integer arguments in parentheses invokes the constructor that specifies size and initial value, while using braces invokes the `std::initializer_list` constructor, creating a vector containing those two integers as elements. This subtle syntactic difference leads to vastly different objects.

The common pitfall is assuming that braces and parentheses are interchangeable for constructor calls. Developers may choose braced initialization for its consistency, only to find their code is calling an unexpected constructor and producing incorrect results. This is particularly dangerous because the code often still compiles, leading to runtime logic errors instead of build-time failures.
practical_example: Initializing `std::vector<int> v(5, 10);` creates a vector containing ten 5s. In contrast, `std::vector<int> v{5, 10};` creates a vector containing two elements: 5 and 10. A developer switching between these syntaxes without understanding the `std::initializer_list` preference can introduce subtle and serious bugs.
